utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We continue, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Your Honours. Please allow me before I start, Your Honour, because yesterday there wasn't enough time, just for the record, a witness Father Jovo Lakic was previously on the list of defendant Miroslav Tadic and since I put him on my list for a character witness I just want to have that for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Because defendant Miroslav Tadic just -- I mean father, he is not on the list any more --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: -- on defendant Tadic, so it was just a small change within these numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. I'm sure the Prosecution have noticed that and they have no objection. They would have raised it earlier. MR. DI FAZIO: No. Yes, that's so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic, you have half an hour to complete your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Pantelic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Ninkovic.

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified yesterday about activities in terms of your work in the field of information. Tell me, you spoke about Odzak too, of course, and the problems of the detained Serbs and the month of May. Tell me, do you know about the Crisis Staff reaching a decision in the month of May about isolating the Croat population and placing on vital facilities in May, 1992, checkpoints in the town of Samac?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Ninkovic, did you personally know about an incident or rather a crime committed in Crkvina sometime during the first half of the month of May, 1992, when within a warehouse, about 15 non-Serb civilians were killed? If you know about this, could you tell us about it and could you tell us who you found out from?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about this. There was no official report or information about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Was this talked about among the population?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A bit later, there was some talk, but all of it was hearsay. There was a war going on. There is a lot of misinformation going on during a war, any way, so the story about this crime was something that I could neither believe nor disbelieve.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me when, in which period, you heard these rumours?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is considerably later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Give us an approximation of the time involved?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps two or three months later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Ninkovic, at that time, May of 1992, could you just remind me, your position then, were you working with Mr. Simeon Simic with regards to information and were you at that time publishing this bulletin you mentioned yesterday, where you were recording news of what was going on in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that I worked in the field of information and that I worked on that job with Mr. Simeon Simic; that is to say, I cooperated with him. This was the end of April, I don't know exactly on which day, but that's when we started issuing that bulletin, perhaps 20 something of April. I can't define the exact date. That's when we started publishing this bulletin. It was not coming out all the time. It came out, say, ten or 15 times at the most. These were brief news flashes on one or two pages and the page format was A4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you. And this incident in Crkvina was not reported by anyone who was working with you or for you and Mr. Simic -- Mr. Simeon Simic for that bulletin? There was no news of this incident published? Or was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that bulletin, this particular news was not published because I said that there was no report, no information from the MUP or from the military authorities, and they were the ones who were in charge of reporting about that. However, we could not publish anything about such an event without having some information that would have been reliable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said, Mr. Ninkovic, that that was two or three months later. Tell me, what are the details that you learned then, two or three months later?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found out about this from the representative of the 1st Krajina Corps. It is well known that in this area of Posavina, the units of the 1st Krajina Corps came sometime in the beginning of July. This was a significant, large, powerful military force. They came, and they started questioning people, they started bringing in volunteers from Serbia, and that is when people started talking about this more. Then there was more information about this, and that is when I heard more about that particular event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned these volunteers from Serbia. Tell me, what was their attitude towards the civilian population, like in Samac?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They instilled fear in people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, what was their attitude towards the municipal officials, towards the civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The civilian authorities also feared these people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Ninkovic, Operation Corridor, when did that happen? Can you give us an approximation of the time involved?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Operation Corridor was towards the end of June, 1992, and that is when the corridor was broken through by Modrica and Gajevica. I think on the 26th or the 27th of June, or perhaps on the 28th, the units of the Army of Republika Srpska were linked up, that is to say those from the 1st Krajina Corps and the units from the East Bosnian Corps or rather the 2nd Posavina Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether military administration then came into being in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, in the autumn of 1992, do you have any knowledge about a particular incident when the army arrested Stevan Todorovic and Milan Simic?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I went to Brcko on official business and there was a military police checkpoint at the entrance into about Brcko. I was stopped there. When the police stopped me, a military policeman walked up to me, a man whom I knew, that was Lazar Stanisic. An assemblyman in the Municipal Assembly of Samac. I knew that man well. He walked up to me and said that the two of them had been arrested, and he told me how miserable and small they were in prison when they were beaten up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you know about closing the corridor after this arrest?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in Crkvina, as far as I know. These are members of the 2nd Posavina Brigade. I think that they were under the leadership of that group of volunteers that we talked about. Afterwards, when talking to Milan Dupljanin, Commander of the 1st Tactical Group, I heard that they had received information that the corridor was broken through by Samac, and they set out with a significant military force, armoured vehicles, combat vehicles, et cetera, in order to deal with the situation, but later on, when they arrived there, it turned out that it was something different that had happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In respect of these occurrences, were any court proceedings initiated at the time?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, before the military Prosecutor's Office in Banja Luka, there were proceedings against some persons from this group of volunteers, but I don't know what the epilogue was of these court proceedings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could we have Exhibit P127, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we get the document, could you tell me what you know about a certain piece of information signed by a number of military personnel, sometime in late autumn, 1992? Tell me, do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In view of my position, I often went to the brigade command, to the personnel service, where I talked about our official business. Mostly concerning the mobilisation of personnel, technical equipment, records. So that is the line of work in which we had cooperation. I got some closer information in terms of the existence of such information and later on it was confirmed that such information did exist. I'm trying to say here, as a person who worked in a government agency and whose job was to enforce the law, that the commander of the 2nd Posavina Brigade, Mr. Mile Beronja, did not deal with his professional obligations properly. I think that he should not allow questions that are outside the law on defence to be placed on the agenda of the brigade command because these are civilian matters. In the law on the army, there is no mention that the brigade command can deal with civilian affairs. There were assistant commanders at the command of the corps for contacts with civilian authorities. I knew, and I do know, Mr. Novica Simic, Commander of the corps. He is a general now. He always had words of praise for the contribution of the civilian authorities in Samac, to the army primarily material resources, that is to say fuel, food, et cetera. So in my opinion, Lieutenant Colonel Mile Beronja was not supposed to allow the command of the brigade to discuss matters that belong to the field of civilian affairs. There is no support for this in the law anywhere. It is unprofessional.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Ninkovic, what do you know about the background, about the motives for writing this information? But please, could you just give shorter answers because we still have a few subjects to deal with.

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that some forces defeated at the first free elections held in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1990 tried, through the authorities of the military, where there was a real concentration of power, to assume power.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you say something about the attempts to convene a session of the Municipal Assembly at the time, and do you know who made these attempts?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not an assemblyman in the Municipal Assembly. I know that when the first session was convened, there was a broad debate on this subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yeah. When the first Assembly was convened, can we have the time period, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, are we talking about the period -- I mean which period in 1992 are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was at that Assembly. I think it was the beginning of 1993. Although preparations were being carried out as far back as November, December. I think it was in January or February, but I cannot give the exact date. This was in Pisari.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A very concrete question in relation to this information: Were there any requests there to convene the Assembly? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in this particular information?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no, no. On the occasion of this information or due to this information in respect of that subject, did anybody trying to convene this Assembly?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I didn't really understand what you were saying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So who did?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lazar Stanisic member of the military police the one I mentioned a few minutes ago he was an assemblyman and he was really the one who was channelling this activity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did all this end?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a failure because not enough signatures were collected because the rules of procedure of the Municipal Assembly stipulate how an assembly meeting can be convened. This Assembly meeting was convened by Blagoje Simic and there was a broad discussion on this subject and I know that this illegal attempt was condemned then. We can say that this was outside the rules of procedure of the Municipal Assembly. Let me say to you that an assemblyman has the right to initiate a meeting, but he has a gather a certain number of signatures. So it is not illegal, but it went beyond the rules of procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to certain portions of this testimony. I let it go previously a few minutes ago. I have no objection to him offering certain conclusions relating to military matters, but he keeps on saying that this was, with regard to this Assembly, that this was an illegal attempt, with regards to the acts of Mile Beronja, he said it was an illegal action. This man is not a lawyer. There is no evidence of legal training. There is no evidence of any legal expertise that he has. As a result, it be the Prosecution's request that he not offer any legal opinions. He is a fact witness. If he would like to offer his military opinions, that's fine, but when he starts -- he's continually offered legal opinions and that's outside the scope of his expertise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, I believe that this witness during his education, was in contact with the laws, army laws, military laws. If he is speaking about the position of Commander Beronja, who is one of the authors of this letter, he surely be in a situation to know what are the scope of authority is for Commander Beronja and for the others. In that sense, I think that he's perfectly entitled to give his opinion, because his education was related to the army legislations. And another thing with regard to the illegal conclusions of the Assembly, parliament, municipal parliament in Samac or the meeting, I can clarify that with the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, because --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That's his personal knowledge or his conclusion, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. It's important to remember that he's a fact witness and I know that with regard to some issues, there can be a very, very thin line between opinion and fact evidence but please do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ninkovic, please tell me, do you know anything about what was the motive and what was behind the attempt to convene the Assembly? Please tell us whether you learned about this from your fellow citizens, from people from civilian authorities. Give us the basis for this information, where did you obtain it, so that we are sure this is not some conclusion of yours about the parliamentary life?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found this out from the assemblymen in the Municipal Assembly of Samac. I knew all of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Give us some names?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: David Simic, Perica Hrstanovic, Simeon Simic, Lazar Lazarvic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We can continue. Please tell us, what do you know about the fact that in April, 1992, or starting from April, 1992, until the summer of 1992, a number of non-Serb residents of Samac were arrested. What do you know about this?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've told you that in my contacts with Mr. Milos Savic, I learned that a number of people had been arrested, that they had been detained and investigated, that unlawful items had been found in their possession, meaning weapons and plans of paramilitary nature and that there was a police investigation instigated against them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you learn from somebody else as well that there were these cases of arrests and what was the basis for them?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Let me tell you, I was involved in military affairs, especially in April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I mean April and on. Did anybody else from the police tell you about that?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was the most specific information I got. I didn't have any other information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any contacts with Savo Cancarevic?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. However, he didn't say it to me explicitly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean he didn't say it to you explicitly? Can you explain that? Did he say anything to you?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what did he say?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that they had orders to arrest some people. However, he didn't mention names, numbers and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ninkovic, please tell me, when was it that you learned for the first time about certain incidents and criminal deeds committed by Stevan Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned about it in 1996, when the indictment was issued.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Starting in April, 1992, until late 1993, did you know about individual crimes and individual acts committed by Stevan Todorovic in Samac?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How can you describe the relationship between Stevan Todorovic, as Chief of Police in Samac, and other members of local civil authorities, other local officials, that's what I mean? If you can give us, please, your view of that and your personal -- and your personal information?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will give you my opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not opinion, Mr. Ninkovic. Give us facts. Please tell us about events where you were an eyewitness in 1992 and 1993. An opinion is one thing and facts are something quite different. What do you know about this?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stevan Todorovic was a person with an excessive amount of energy that he was unable to control always. He frequently imposed his views and positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1992 and 1993, did Stevan Todorovic use alcohol?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was his behaviour then?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would just exacerbate his lack of control. He would become aggressive at times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you personally know about his relationship with some local officials? Was he on friendly terms with them? How would you explain his relationship with them?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't really respect anybody much. He simply was not somebody who was of a cooperative nature. He never worked before the war except for a year or a year and a half, when he worked in Korpora as an engineer for wood processing. So he has very little experience in state administration and police in state organs. So that was basically a very bad appointment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, was there a camp in Zasavica for non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That couldn't be called a camp. That was some kind of an isolation site.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Ninkovic, could you explain what is the difference between a camp and an isolation site, in your words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I never visited a single facility where detainees were held. In my career, up until now, I've never visited a single prison, so my knowledge is strictly theoretical. A camp is -- or a prison is a place where strict discipline is enforced, where there is a police or military supervision, where there are harsh conditions, under which people are kept, in terms of food they receive, sanitary conditions and so on. Isolation, on the other hand, is a different concept. People are put away due to security reasons or some other reasons, and people can move free about in a certain area but cannot leave that area. Zasavica, was, for example a village and these people were unable to leave the village without a permit. However, within the village itself, they could move about freely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there barbed wire around Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any checkpoints with armed guards around Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just clarify this. As far as I know, Zasavica was a place to the right of the main road, Samac-Modrica. There were frequent members -- there were frequent situations where police officers or troops would move on the road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, were there any Serbs in Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were these Serbs from?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were refugees who had come from central Bosnia. I think it was the village of Gostovic, Bistrica and some other places. These people fled those areas and were housed in that village, in the houses there, together with Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they lived together in Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned freedom of movement and passes, permits. Can you tell me, please, who was in charge of issuing permits and regulating movement of civilian population in Samac in 1992 and 1993? Who issued such permits and passes?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, at the beginning, various organs were issuing passes and permits. I think the MUP did, as did the Crisis Staff at the beginning. Then in early autumn, the government of Republika Srpska realising that there was a problem in the field, that this field had not been regulated --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. Let's do this briefly. In 1992 and 1993, who issued permits to civilians and who issued them to military personnel?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pursuant to that government decree, in -- military organs were issuing passes for troops. Members of the MUP were issued permits by the Ministry of interior, whereas the civilian population, those who had work obligation, were issued permits by the organ of the Ministry of the Defence as was the case with passports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Serbs who were refugees and who lived in Zasavica in 1992 and 1993, did they have to have permits in order to move about?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did all of the residents of Samac municipality have to have permits in order to move about the municipality in the times of war?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you personally have any information about the activities of municipal officials in 1992 and 1993 that were aimed at ethnic discrimination of non-Serb population in Samac?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, the time is up. I actually allowed ten minutes over because we started a little late.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Only, Your Honour, the last question, very last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Finally.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Finally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tell me, please, briefly, you have experience in journalism and so on. What can you tell me briefly about Blagoje Simic as a man whom you know?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Blagoje Simic is a family man, he's family oriented. He was a withdrawn, quiet person. He was cooperative and willing to solve problems. He's an intellectual, a physician, a humanist, who at the time was quite young and lacked experience in politics. It was a difficult period of time. The war had just started. And I don't believe that he always had good assistance in various matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ninkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Cross-examination? Oh, I'm sorry, Mr. Lukic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will attempt to be as brief as possible. I have a total of six documents that I would like to introduce through this witness. This witness has touched upon these documents already and I would like to cover this as quickly as possible. I've prepared these documents for the Trial Chamber, for the Registry. This has to do with some topics that had already been raised in respect to questions put by Mr. Pantelic. However I will not repeat them. I will just put the questions that I'm interested in. Cross-examined by Mr. Lukic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ninkovic, what I've heard from your testimony is that you're an engineer of civilian protection. I've heard that before the war, you were an expert in civilian defence and could you please explain that concept to the Trial Chamber? The first thing I'd like to know is how did the civilian protection function before the war, and very briefly, please tell us who was in charge of establishing civilian protection, who appointed officials within that institution, and then please explain the term of commissioner for civilian Defence, because I didn't like the interpretation -- the translation in the English language, so please explain what the commissioner is, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shall we start from the last question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. Please tell us whether civilian protection existed as a concept before the war and how was it regulated?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, civilian protection is a part of the defence system; that is, an unarmed component of the defence which consists of civilian protection staff, units, and commissioners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm interested in that term of "commissioner" for civilian defence?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A commissioner is a citizen appointed by the civilian protection staff for a segment of the street, for a hamlet, for a part of a village, or for an apartment building. That person has a duty to inform other residents of an imminent threat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, please tell me, what regulation, before the war, regulated the area of civilian defence and who appointed officials to civilian protection organs?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pursuant to law -- or the law on defence regulated the civilian protection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the municipal level who decided on appointments?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're referring to the pre-war period, civilian protection staff appointed the executive council [As interpreted].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean? Of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell me, do you know what regulations regulate civilian defence in Republika Srpska? I'm especially interested in 1992 and 1993.

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once the law on defence was adopted, and it was announced on the 8th of June, 1992, this regulated the subject of civilian defence and at the end of September --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. Sorry to interrupt. I think there is a mistake in the transcript. On page 17 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: It says, line 24, the question is if you're referring to the pre-war period, civilian protection staff, appointed the executive council, should that be was appointed by the executive council? You have the civilian defence appointing members of the executive council. I think that's incorrect, the interpretation. That's lines 23 and 24.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I'm sure Mr. Lukic can clear that up.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank my colleague from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So let us clarify this for the sake of language. Who appointed the civilian protection staff?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The executive council of the Municipal Assembly of Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we interrupted you. What happened in the month of September?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In September, a by-law was published, that is to say the decree on civilian protection, which defined more clearly the rights and responsibilities of the authorities and members of the civilian defence.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please pause before putting his question?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would now like to you clarify another thing here before the Trial Chamber. Tell us, what is the difference between Territorial Defence and the civilian protection? Did both exist before the war and what is their interrelationship in the system of armed forces?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The difference is a substantive one. The Territorial Defence is part of the armed forces of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia; that is to say, that there were units and weapons. That is to say, this was a real force, whereas the civilian protection is the unarmed component of the defence system. Its basic objective is to protect persons and property in a state of emergency. That is to say, when there are natural disasters, technological disasters of large proportions, like fires, oil spills, et cetera, and war, by the very nature of things, is a state of emergency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that the civilian protection has a special role in case of war?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next thing I'm interested in, now we are moving to the period of 1992, when the law on defence regulated this and we go further on. Can members of the civilian protection issue any kind of orders to the military or to the police?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Civilian protection, as an institution, does it have any powers in terms of detention?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does civilian protection have any powers in terms of the judiciary and investigation organs?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned yesterday and during the previous days those coordinators of work units. Do you remember whether their premises were at the retirees home in Samac for a while? Do you remember any of that?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you perhaps remember where their premises were in this building? Was it on the ground floor or the first floor?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not enter so I cannot testify about any details of this respect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember whether they moved later to another building, whether their offices went elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you talking about the civilian protection headquarters?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I'm talking about the coordinators of the work unit.

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they stayed there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You probably know that that is where the headquarters of the civilian defence were as well?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this headquarters have its seat elsewhere, then?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. Your Honour, I have a problems with the following transcript. In one part of the explanations, what we have receiving as an English translation here, there is inconsistence with the terms and I believe that this term is quite important for these proceedings. My colleague, Mr. Lukic is always using a word, "service for civilian defence." I don't know in English what is the more appropriate civil defence or civil protection, but let's clarify that and let's stick to one term. Up to the page 20, line 20, it was civilian protection, but suddenly, it's civilian defence. It might be to some extent confusing. So I kindly ask our interpreters to give us a precise term in English language for term which was used in these proceedings for civilian defence or protection, I don't know. It's a part of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I'm sure Mr. Lukic will pick that up.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it would be best to use the term that was already given officially by the translation service in various documents, and civil protection is the word that was used in the official translations of documents that we are going to analyse now. So I would like to suggest to the interpreters to the -- to use that term.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The civil protection headquarters, could it give any orders to these coordinators of the work units, or could they, as every other user of that unit, did it just turn with its request to them?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The civil protection headquarters could ask for the engagement of members of the work obligation units, and companies and institutions, to help them resolve certain problems. So it could request units from the work obligation and for work obligation from companies because civil protection uses material resources from the inventory, that is to say, when clearing of rubble is concerned, then they use the construction machinery of construction companies. They do not have any special material, technical equipment. They use what is from the inventory.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters kindly ask counsel not to speak at the same time when the witness is speaking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They cooperate with the executive council at all levels because it has control over municipal enterprises and it can also order the use of machinery, tools, from enterprises for the needs of civil protection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, remember to pause and also allow the answer of the witness to be completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We didn't receive the last question, the interpreter was speaking when the question was being read and could we just find out what this question was that this witness just responded to with an answer? The answer is at line 4 on page 22. No question. Mr. Lukic speaking while the interpreter was speaking so question was ever issued so we are trying to figure out what the answer means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question was the same like in line 21, I repeated 16. So could civil protection give orders to anyone? But the witness answered and there is no need for any repetition. You also mentioned yesterday or the other day, when speaking to Pantelic, you mentioned the building of concrete bunkers for the military. I would like to know whether you have any knowledge about the civil protection as an institution having anything to do with these concrete bunkers for the military. Did they ask for people or did they do anything in this respect?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown document C59? That is the law on defence. This is a document that the Prosecution wanted to introduce during the pre-trial stage but they obviously gave up on it. Sir, it is the law on defence of Republika Srpska from the 1st of June, 1992. I just handed it in. It's the first document. You have already referred to this law, Mr. Ninkovic. You mentioned it to me just a short while ago. I don't want to analyse it very specifically now because the document speaks for itself as it were, but I would like to know from your practice, that is to say from the practice of your department, of the ministry, could you please give me a comment with regard to two or three particular articles? Obviously, this is a system based law and you yourself said that after that, probably in different fields, it was regulated in different ways what is mentioned in this regulation. Article 13, I am going to read it. I have given the original to the interpreters as well. It is very brief. "The Ministry of Defence orders carrying out certain tasks and duties related to work obligation for the needs of defence in accordance with the decree adopted by the government." Did you mean -- MR. DI FAZIO: I do apologise to my learned friend, there is just one matter he raised in his preamble to the question. And that is this: Mr. Lukic said that this particular document is regulated in different ways. Am I to understand or is the Chamber to understand that the application of the laws contained in this particular gazette were applied differently in different places and under different circumstances from that comment made by Mr. Lukic? It just went in and it's unclear to me what he meant by that, and whether the witness will in fact give an answer to it. But it's a matter that's something that you should know about, if indeed this is applied differently in different circumstances, it might be important in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic, can we have an explanation?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this is a misinterpretation, and I didn't want to ask the witness to go into a legal interpretation. When I said system-based law, I wanted to say that this law regulated many fields that stem from this law and that there were by-laws on this basis so I'm going to ask the witness about what he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ninkovic, after this law was passed, in different fields that are mentioned in this law, were there any new regulations that were adopted and who adopted these regulations, very briefly please?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In this law, you have the rights and responsibilities of the government of Republika Srpska. There is a special chapter where it says specifically what the duties of the government of Republika Srpska are. I think that this is Article 7 or 8 of the law. Here it is. It is Article 8 of this law. So the government, on the basis of Article 8 of this law, regulates in greater detail the field of defence by way of decrees. Decrees are by-laws which do not have to be adopted by the Assembly. They are adopted by the government as an executive organ. That is a well-known technology in the work of state institutions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, could we have that on the ELMO for the benefit of our clients also. And another thing, I need the assistance of the technical unit because I don't receive both on this place, I don't have anything from the ELMO. So I personally cannot follow the proceedings. There is no signal, neither on the left nor on the -- I am not receiving. Nobody is receiving here from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: We are not receiving anything from the ELMO on the bench either.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I have already requested for technician assistance, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am going to read this brief article once again and this way the accused are going to be aware of what I'm asking you about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is Article 13. It reads as follows: "The Ministry of Defence orders the discharge of tasks and duties related to work obligation for defence needs in accordance with the decree that is adopted by the government." And we also referred to Article 3 -- Article 8, line 3, and Mr. Pantelic referred to it as well?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Article that you read, 13, is of a -- is of a general nature and then the government does this on the -- specifically on the basis of decrees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did it do it?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 28th of September, 1992, if you're referring to civil protection. That's when that decree came out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about work obligation? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as work obligation is concerned, there were several decrees at different points in time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We are going to move on to what I'm interested in now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Lukic, before we do, just going back to the term "civil protection" versus "civil defence," in the document, the English translation we have in front of us, in fact the term civil defence is used continually through the translation. So I just put that on the record, because it's at odds with what we were saying before the term "civil protection" maybe should be used for consistency. Part 5, for example, which details civil defence and the various things to do with it, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, Judge Williams. I have referred to a document that I'm going to analyse subsequently with the witness, and that is the decree on the organisation of civil protection, where the word civil protection is used. And obviously -- but I think that the Trial Chamber, when they read the regulations involved, are probably going to get an impression themselves as to what this term actually denotes. I mentioned civil protection because that is what was used in the decree but then obviously in the law a different term was used so... Both protection and defence mean the same thing as zastita does in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. That's what we understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ninkovic, the entire chapter of this law is devoted to civilian protection. We are not going to analyse it or read it. Just please comment briefly on Article 36. Since ELMO is not working, I will read it out for the sake of the accused: "In order to protect and rescue people, property, cultural heritage and other assets from destruction by war, natural and other major disasters, in times of peace or war, the following civil defence tasks shall be carried out. One, providing shelter for and evacuating people, property and cultural heritage; two, blackout; three, providing shelter for those at risk and casualties; four, radiological, chemical and biological protection; five, protection from collapsing structures and rescue from the rubble; six, protection and rescue from floods and on water; seven, protection and rescue from fire and explosions; eight, first aid; nine, protection and salvage of food and animals; ten, cleanup. Peace time fire fighting shall be carried out in accordance with a special law." And the last paragraph is: "The Minister of Defence shall issue detailed regulations on the implementation of civil defence tasks." All of this was later regulated by various regulations. Now, please tell me whether these tasks of civil defence were set out in pre-war period by the law on armed forces of SFRY and did the ministry pass any other detailed regulations?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was regulated before the war and the law was called the law on people's defence. It was not called the law on armed forces. These are two different laws.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that the Ministry of Defence subsequently passed regulations to implement these tasks?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we are referring to 1992, meaning after the decree that I've mentioned, the decree that was passed in September of 1992, after that, there followed instructions from the Ministry of Defence, and instructions are a lower enactment than a decree.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I need your comment on Article 36. I will read paragraph 3: "Heads of district civil protection staffs are appointed and removed from office."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It's not 36. It's actually Article 46.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. There is a mistake there. Can we start again, Mr. Lukic, please, and read slowly?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Article 46, paragraph 3: "Chiefs and members of the regional civilian defence staffs are appointed and removed from office by the commander of civilian protection staff of the republic." Since you told us about the pre-war procedure, is this how it was based on pre-war legislation?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did it look in practice after the law was adopted?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civil protection staff had members for various sectors that you've read out. Those are experts for various fields. For example, for the field of protection of animals, usually a veterinarian is appointed. For the first aid, a physician is appointed. For saving people out of rubble, a civilian engineer. For evacuation, somebody who is familiar with the social protection. So this is a team composed of experts for various fields in accordance with the measures that you've read out previously. However, there was no commander but rather a chief. That's how it used to be. The chief is an expert, is an operative, who leads the staff. However, decisions are passed by the entire body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember perhaps until what time Miroslav Tadic was commander of civilian protection staff?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the fall of 1992, but I cannot give you a more precise date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like this document to be admitted into evidence unless the Prosecution has any objections? MR. DI FAZIO: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. Can we have the number, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit D79/3 and D79/3 ter for the B/C/S. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Another document that you've already mentioned before, and I would like us to analyse now, is a decree on organising and functioning of civilian protection dated 29 September, 1992. MR. DI FAZIO: Could we have the number of the -- the private number that Defence and Prosecution are using between themselves?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry, my friend. It's PDB 54/3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since in your previous testimony, you've already said quite a bit regarding this decree, I will now read just two paragraphs of Article 29. These are the last two paragraphs in Article 29 of this decree, that read as follows: "Civilian protection staff shall consist of Chief of Staff, Assistant Chiefs of Staff, professional consultants and administrative and technical staff in keeping with the personnel and material establishment. Civilian protection staffs must include representatives of water and power supply companies, post and telecommunications, public utilities enterprises, the burial service, oil industry, traffic, and transportation, health care, veterinary services, protection of plants, the media, seismology, fire protection, the police, the army, and other vital services." I assume that this is what you've just told us.

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Civilian protection staff, when members are nominated for the staff, it is always done on the basis that civilian protection staff should comprise experts, and you've just numbered out the fields that the staff needs to have experts from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what you know about the function of representatives of police and army within the civilian protection staffs? What was their role and their duty in that staff?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are no representatives of police and army in the civilian protection staffs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I've just read out some paragraphs from Article 29, where it says that they send their representatives. Do you know whether in Samac, in civilian protection staff, there were representatives of police and army?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not before the war and not afterwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like this document to be given a number, if there are no objections. MR. DI FAZIO: No, no objection, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can we have the number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The microphone. It's D80/3 and D80/3 ter for the Serbo-Croat one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since in these regulations another service is mentioned, that you have mentioned as well, and it is quite important for my case, could you please tell us what is the service for monitoring and reporting? What is its task? Did it exist before the war and what is its role? But before you tell us that, was this usually referred to in Samac as communications centre?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were its premises?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the building in downtown, the building was known as the SDK building or rather the bank building, because on the ground floor, there were offices of the bank and then upstairs was the centre for communications. The official term from the legislation is report -- monitoring and reporting centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it have an abbreviation?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. COO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that upon arriving to Samac, you went to that centre first. Please tell us, what is the role of that service?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This centre was within the Secretariat for People's Defence. They had an alarm siren there and the button to activate it, and if the button was activated, the sirens would go off. There were several sirens in town and there were several types of signal. One was for air raids; one was for natural emergencies; one signal was for the end of threat, of toxic spills and so on. So these were kinds of signals. And there were also instructions for residents to be able to distinguish among these signals. This centre would activate the siren for air raid and if -- this siren would go on if there was a threat or after the attack began, the air raid attack. That was of vital importance for civilian population because by activating this signal, the residents were warned that they need to seek shelter and therefore avoid casualties. This centre gave a great contribution to protection of civilians from shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise for interruption. It's just for the clarity of transcript, Your Honour. There witness said on page 31, line 22, he said that centre for "O" and "O," this is abbreviation. And I don't see that in transcript. So I would like that my colleague, Mr. Lukic clarify that. Because otherwise, it's quite confusing in line 18 and 19, he said yes, COO. And then he mentioned that, how the right abbreviation is, but it is not in the transcript. On B/C/S, in his native language, he mentioned that but I don't see that in the English version. Could you clarify that, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic, please clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the abbreviation slowly?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said the abbreviation?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, the abbreviated name?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: CO, small case i, upper case O. COiO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like now to turn to another topic that has been mentioned before. I don't want to repeat, but I would like to introduce the document with an internal number RH1, and this is a document of the Prosecution. I would like to hear your comment on this decree on control of persons, vehicles and goods. This decree is from October of 1992, the 2nd of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown the document, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've already testified about this so we are not going to spend much time on it. The document is self-explanatory. Article 2 sets forth what you said about members of police and army. Article 3 deals with those people who had work obligation. And Article 4 deals with civilians and the other categories of population. Could you please tell us, those citizens that were not engaged in work obligation, what was the procedure if they wanted it leave not just the territory of the town, but to leave Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The procedure was as follows: The resident would have to come to the department for defence, submit a short written request on a form that had already been preprinted so a citizen would just have to fill it in and sign, specify the reason for travelling, destination, a number of days that he or she intends to spend there, and then on the same day, he or she would be issued a pass. The reason could be medical treatment, visit to family members and so on. Just basically private affairs that all citizens have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this pertain to all citizens regardless of their ethnic origin?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, to all of them, irrespective of their ethnic origin. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, it might be important for you to obtain from this witness, and perhaps I'm jumping the gun here, maybe Mr. Lukic is going to ask him about this, but is the witness's position simply that if you wanted to get out, all you had to do is go to the Ministry of Defence, get your permission and leave? If that's his position, we should be clear about that because of course it's significant in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The way he has explained it is that you put it in writing. MR. DI FAZIO: Okay. Put it in writing, but if you want to leave, that's what you do. I think we should be absolutely crystal clear about that, for obvious reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to admit that the -- this comment of the Prosecutor is not quite clear to me, but if I made a mistake that can be corrected during cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Citizens, irrespective of their ethnic origin could have their own free will apply to leave the area and those who were not covered by the work obligation, did they have to specify reasons for leaving and those who had a work obligation, did other rules apply to them? We obviously have different categories here.

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm confused by the question put by the Prosecutor and your question. So I am not quite sure what you need, but that was a typical procedure that was used on a daily basis, and every civilian citizen, meaning somebody who was not a member of MUP or of the army, and who wanted to travel, had to have a pass, because at checkpoints, a pass needed to be shown. Therefore, those who had a decision on work obligation in their pass there was specified when they needed to return, meaning that once their personal affairs were completed, they needed to return to continue performing their work obligation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These passes, were they valid for the territory of Croatia, or the Federation? If somebody wanted to travel there?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where could these passes only be used?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the territory of Republika Srpska, Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and abroad, third countries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, if somebody wanted to go to Croatia or to the Federation, what was the only way of leaving Samac?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A person couldn't travel there with this type of pass.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where would they have to apply to, then?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that they had to apply to the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did they register there for, for what type of commission? Who could take them there?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not quite familiar with these procedures that you want me to discuss here. However, I think that you are referring to the Red Cross, to unification of families. You are referring to people who want to travel to Croatia and the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear of the commission for exchange?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will go back to the previous topic. Do you know that in the centre for communications, during the war, there was some specific events, incidents. What else took place in the centre for communications during the war and why did it take place there particularly?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I will explain that. Before the war, the centre for communications of Samac municipality had a radio connection with several neighbouring municipalities, Gracanica, Doboj, Teslic, Modrica, Odzak, Derventa and Brod. So that's a region. That was connected by radio link. Once the war broke out, this radio link functioned only with respect to some municipalities, among others municipality of Odzak. The only place where one could communicate with people who were in Odzak was through the centre for communications in Odzak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we please be given a number for this document, decree on traffic checks of persons, vehicles and merchandise, if there are no objections from the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit D81/3 and D81/3 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The following document is directly linked to the previous one. Could the witness please be shown document with internal mark DBD 90/3? That's a pass for travel abroad dated 2nd February, 1993. Mr. Ninkovic, is this your signature? Are you familiar with this document? Tell us something about it.

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is my document, meaning that this is a document issued by department of defence of Samac, whose head I was. It has all elements of a regular document. It has a heading, number, date, legal preamble based on which this document is issued. Then you can see here the name of the person petitioning for the pass to be issued, personal data of the petitioner. His or her residence and so on. The period during which the person would be absent. And the reason for issuance of this pass which here is set forth as a visit to the family, travel abroad, and the dates of the travel are mentioned, which, as you can see, is an appropriate time for a travel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the preamble, you referred to Article 3 of the decree, which pertains to people covered by the work obligation. I am now interested in those citizens who did not have a work obligation. Those that are mentioned in Article 4 of the decree. Did you give them a deadline by which they needed to return as well?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that that's how it was. I don't think that there was a time limit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And before the break, please tell us what is the ethnic origin of this person in this pass?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I think it's time for our break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have a number, please, for the document? Any objection from the Prosecution? MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, probably not but I realise that I've not been given the correct document. I haven't seen this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So we will deal with it after the break. We will have a break now and continue our proceedings at 1100 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like my colleague, Mr. Di Fazio, to say whether he was any objections, whether he objects to having this document admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, please. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. Yes. I realise -- I do apologise. I have no objection to the admission of that document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. Yes. Can we have the number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit D82/3 and D82/3 ter for the B/C/S. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ninkovic, one more question related to the previous document. Its date is the 2nd of February, 1993. Can you tell me until when these permits were issued? All the way up to the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the way up to the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And approximately how often were they issued?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Irrespective of ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, irrespective of ethnic background, religion, any citizen who came obtained a permit of this nature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next document I would like the witness to be shown is document that is internally marked PDB 61/3 [As interpreted]. That is a permit for travel and movement dated the 3rd of November, 1992. I'm correcting the interpreter. The document is internally marked PDB 61/2. Since the works now, could you please place the document on the ELMO so that the accused could see them, too, the documents, or these two documents, obviously. It's one document copied twice, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a permit issued by the Army of Republika Srpska, command of Tactical Group 1. They were stationed in Odzak. The Commander was Milan Dupljanin, a person I know. And in order for someone to move about this area of Odzak within the area of responsibility of Tactical Group 1, they would have to have this kind of permit. In my testimony so far, I have said that I was personally brought in because I did not have a permit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this permit exclusively for that area that was the area of responsibility of the 1st Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there are no objections from the Prosecution I would like to have this document admitted into evidence now. MR. DI FAZIO: No objection, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit D83/3 and D83/3 ter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next document that I would like the witness to be shown is document internally marked PDB 142/3. This is a decree on work obligation issued by the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina dated the 10th of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ninkovic, during your testimony these past few days, you said that often you were in contact with your colleagues from the other entity, that you know that the legal regulations in various fields were similar because you all relied on the pre-war documents and legislation of the former Yugoslavia; That is to say, before 1992. Do you have any knowledge about this document? Just a minute, please because the Prosecutor wants to ask something?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right, you may proceed. MR. DI FAZIO: I don't object to the question if it's confined to "Do you have any knowledge about this document?" If he's just asking that and as we understand that is simply the question, no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The contact I had after the war with persons who were involved in a similar line of work as I am and they are from the other entity I heard from them that then they also relied on legal strongholds from the former laws of the socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, giving legal opinions on the basis of what he's heard from other people is -- A, it's imprecise and it's not a matter to be permitted, I submit. You need something far more precise than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: He's -- from the answer he simply says that the other people told him that they too relied on the legal strongholds, that's all. There is no opinion involved. MR. DI FAZIO: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I clarify this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In a bit more detail? You see, we who worked in Bosnia-Herzegovina in the Ministry of Defence, in the Secretariat of the Ministry of Defence, there were ethnic communities there, or rather persons from the ethnic communities, all three of them, as a matter of fact. When the war broke out, professionals in a way had the same knowledge irrespective of their ethnic background and they drew on the same experience and the same knowledge from the same regulations and they built this, incorporated it either into the laws of the Federation or of Republika Srpska. These are persons who went through the same schools, the same courses, the same seminars and worked in the same offices.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Furthermore, with regard to this question, did your colleagues tell you, these colleagues, tell you that in the territory under the Federation, was this regulated in the same way as it was in Republika Srpska accept?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see this document before? Perhaps?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to have this document admitted into evidence if the Prosecution does not object? MR. DI FAZIO: Well, quite probably not, if Your Honours please, but I'm afraid we don't have a copy here. At least the case manager has looked for the document, and we simply haven't -- we haven't received it. So may I just briefly look at it and I can inform you, if Your Honours would just give me a moment, please? Could I ask that it go in, simply be marked for identification at this stage rather than consume the Court's time now with us reading it? It may be that once I've had a chance to look at it, and digest its contents, there will be no objection and we can simply have the document admitted at that stage, but at this stage, without having had a chance to look at it carefully, I can't say. May I say that my initial impression is probably we won't be objecting to its admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well, we'll have it numbered for identification only. MR. DI FAZIO: And I might ask for a copy to be provided by defence of the B/C/S and the English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be marked as document D84/3 ID and D84/3 ter ID. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have concluded my examination-in-chief of this witness, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it will be very brief. Cross-examined by Mr. Lazarevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Ninkovic.

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have just one question for you. From the answers you gave to date it was my understanding that you know Simo Zaric, that you worked on certain matters together, that you had some contacts with him during the war. During 1992, did Simo Zaric ever address you as the municipal Secretary for National Defence, with some request related to engaging a work brigade, any workforce, for the use of the military? I'm interested in Simo Zaric personally.

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have documents to tender through this witness and I would like the assistance of the usher. Unfortunately she's not here at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I hope you gave some to the Prosecution already.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was already everything discussed with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, for the benefit of the Prosecution the first document I would like to discuss with this witness is PDB 4/4.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ninkovic, I'm not going to ask you anything special about this document. I would just like to know, this is a letter addressed to the command of the 2nd Posavina Brigade on the 3rd of December, 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Would you please place it on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says, "Chief, Bozo Ninkovic." And that is what it says by the signature and tell me is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you the person who wrote this letter and sent it to the command of the 2nd Posavina Brigade?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: If there is no objection from our colleagues from the OTP, I with like this document to be admitted into evidence. MR. DI FAZIO: No objection at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can we have the number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit D31/4 and D31/4 ter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And now I would like the witness to be shown the other document that we would like to tender into evidence. MR. DI FAZIO: I wonder, again, for various computer-related reasons, I wonder if Mr. Lazarevic would be so kind as to mention the internal numbering system that we have and so it's in the transcript? It makes it easier for us later to search the transcript when researching the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes. It is number PDB -- are you interested in the document that has already been admitted or the next one? The next one is 3/4.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
